newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire's warring sides due to start peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's warring sides due to start peace talks.

text.p: Zairean government representatives and rebels said on Saturday their first face-to-face talks to end the six-month civil war in the vast African country would start as scheduled at 0800 GMT.

The talks were given new urgency late on Friday by an appeal by the United Nations Security Council to both sides in the conflict to let aid agencies help refugees dying of malnutrition and diseases return home.

"The talks will start at 10 a.m. and they will go on as long as it takes to reach a solution," said Issa Ganda-e-Ndzea, senior Zairean diplomat in South Africa, commenting on the negotiations due to take place at the South African government's headquarters in Pretoria.
"If reaching a solution takes one day, if it takes two days or one month, it doesn't matter. The problem is not the length of the talks. We must just start talking," he told Reuters.
The head of rebel leader Laurent Kabila's delegation, Bizima Karaha, also confirmed the talks would go ahead as planned.

Asked whether he thought the talks would be successful, Karaha, who is also the rebels' foreign affairs commissioner, said: "There's only one and one condition only: the Zaireans must be serious. If they are, the talks will be successful."
Karaha had threatened on Friday to return to Zaire if the government delegation did not demonstrate it was prepared to talk in earnest.
Kabila has insisted that only the removal of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko -- in power for 31 years -- would satisfy his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
Despite diplomatic efforts to broker a ceasefire, central to Saturday's talks, the rebels were continuing their advances in the mining regions of central Zaire on Friday.

Kabila said on Friday his forces, which have seized control of a quarter of the country in just six months, were less than 10 km (6 miles) from diamond capital Mbuji-Mayi after government troops fled.
Rebels have also been slowly encircling Lubumbashi, Zaire's copper-mining hub, which they say is their next target.

In Kinshasa, Mobutu's allies began moves to oust opposition stalwart Etienne Tshisekedi for excluding them from power in his first act since becoming prime minister at the head of a government that hopes to end the civil war.

Diplomats said the controversy triggered by Tshisekedi's appointment -- and his offer of six key cabinet posts to rebels -- had complicated the situation. The rebels have shown open contempt for politicians who have served in Mobutu's government and have flatly turned down the cabinet offer.

Tshisekedi made enemies even among his own supporters in parliament on Thursday by dissolving the transitional assembly. Leaders of the pro-Mobutu FPC parliamentary majority called urgent talks on Friday with the pro-Tshisekedi members to agree strategy on ousting him.
Mobutu, who has cancer, refused to be drawn into the political crisis stirred by Tshisekedi, telling reporters in Kinshasa that this was not the business of the head of state.

South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, a skilled diplomat, puts his credibility on the line when he officially opens the peace talks on Saturday with the joint United Nations and Organisation of African Unity envoy, Mohamed Sahnoun.

Their task was outlined this week by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who told reporters he was hoping the Zairean government and the rebels would set a date for both a ceasefire and proper negotiations during their talks in South Africa.
